title: Skeletal Traction
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Musculoskeletal Injuries

headings.title: Introduction to Skeletal Traction and Its Indications
headings.content: Skeletal traction is an orthopedic intervention used to apply a pulling force directly to a fractured bone through the use of pins, wires, or tongs surgically inserted into the bone. Unlike skin traction, which applies force to the soft tissues, skeletal traction allows for significantly heavier weights and prolonged duration of therapy without causing major soft tissue breakdown. This method is primarily indicated for complex fractures of the femur, tibia, and cervical spine where bone realignment and length restoration are crucial before definitive surgical fixation or healing can occur. For nursing students in Nigeria managing trauma patients in busy orthopedic wards, understanding these indications helps prioritize care for patients awaiting surgery. Skeletal traction is also used to reduce muscle spasms associated with severe fractures, correct or prevent skeletal deformities, and immobilize a specific body part when other methods are contraindicated. The procedure requires strict adherence to aseptic technique during insertion to prevent osteomyelitis. Nurses must recognize that traction is not a treatment for the fracture itself, but a mechanical tool to achieve reduction and alignment. Patient education is initiated early to ensure compliance, as the patient must remain relatively immobile in bed. By understanding the mechanical advantages and clinical indications, nursing students can effectively evaluate why a physician has ordered skeletal traction for a specific patient, ensuring safer and more targeted clinical interventions at the bedside.

headings.title: Anatomy of Pin Sites and Equipment Setup
headings.content: The anatomy surrounding pin sites involves skin, subcutaneous tissue, muscle, periosteum, and bone. When orthopedic pins such as Steinman pins or Kirschner wires are inserted, they traverse these sterile layers, creating a potential pathway for micro-organisms to reach the bone. Common insertion sites include the distal femur, proximal tibia, and the skull for cervical traction. Nursing students must understand that the interface where the metal pin enters the skin is a critical vulnerability point for bacterial entry. Equipment setup for skeletal traction requires precision and specialized hardware, including the pins, a pin insertion drill or hand brace, traction bows (such as a Kirschner or Steinmann bow), ropes, pulleys, and specific weights. The traction rope must be in pristine condition, resting securely within the grooves of the pulleys without fraying or catching. Every component of the setup must be inspected regularly to maintain mechanical integrity. The weights must hang freely above the floor, never resting on the bed frame or floor, as any obstruction alters the prescribed tension. The nurse collaborates with the orthopedic surgeon and physiotherapist during setup to verify that the line of pull is straight and aligned with the long axis of the bone. Maintaining this meticulous equipment setup ensures that the mechanical force applied successfully reduces the fracture without causing soft tissue damage or neurological compromise.

headings.title: Types of Skeletal Traction and Mechanics
headings.content: Skeletal traction operates on fundamental physics and biomechanical principles, primarily Newton's laws of motion, to maintain alignment and counter-traction. For every pulling force applied to the skeletal system, an opposing counter-traction force is required to prevent the patient from sliding down the bed. Counter-traction is typically achieved by using the patient's own body weight by elevating the foot of the bed or utilizing gravity. There are several configurations of skeletal traction, including balanced suspension traction, which supports the affected extremity in a suspended splint while pulling it in a specific direction. Balanced suspension allows the patient to move slightly in bed without interrupting the line of pull or altering the weight on the fracture site. Mechanics dictate that the ropes must remain collinear with the long axis of the bone to ensure that the force vector is accurately directed at the fracture site. Any deviation in the angle of pull can result in malalignment, rotational deformities, or pressure injuries. Nursing students must study these mechanical principles to effectively troubleshoot common traction issues in clinical settings. If a patient complains of sudden pain or if the fracture alignment appears distorted, the nurse must check the rope placement, pulley alignment, and weight position. Understanding mechanics prevents iatrogenic complications and supports optimal orthopedic recovery.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Continuous Monitoring
headings.content: Continuous nursing assessment is vital for patients in skeletal traction to ensure patient safety and early detection of complications. The nurse must perform systematic neurovascular assessments of the affected limb at least every two to four hours, evaluating the five Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, and paralysis. Any sensory loss or diminished capillary refill can indicate compartment syndrome or excessive pressure from dressings or positioning. Skin integrity must also be rigorously monitored, especially over bony prominences such as the sacrum, heels, and elbows, because immobility greatly increases the risk of pressure ulcers. Nurses should assess the patient's pain level using standardized scales, differentiating between expected baseline fracture pain and acute, unrelieved pain that may signal nerve compression or impending vascular compromise. Additionally, psychological assessment is essential, as prolonged immobilization can lead to sensory deprivation, depression, and feelings of helplessness. Respiratory assessment is equally critical; shallow breathing from immobility can cause atelectasis and hypostatic pneumonia, prompting the nurse to encourage deep breathing and coughing exercises every hour. Monitoring fluid balance, bowel habits, and nutritional status rounds out the comprehensive nursing assessment. By maintaining vigilance, nursing students can catch subtle clinical changes before they escalate into life- or limb-threatening emergencies.

headings.title: Pin Site Care and Infection Prevention
headings.content: Pin site care is a cornerstone nursing responsibility aimed at preventing osteomyelitis and localized soft tissue infections around orthopedic pins. Hospital protocols dictate specific frequencies and cleansing agents, such as sterile normal saline or chlorhexidine solutions, used to clean the skin-pin junction. Using a sterile technique, the nurse cleans in a circular motion starting closest to the pin and moving outward, using a fresh swab for each stroke to avoid introducing bacteria closer to the insertion site. Nurses must monitor pin sites for the cardinal signs of infection: redness, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, and severe or worsening pain. A small amount of clear or serosanguinous drainage is normal immediately post-insertion, but thick, foul-smelling pus requires immediate reporting to the surgeon. Crusting around the pin site should generally be left undisturbed unless ordered otherwise, as removing it can disrupt the delicate epithelial seal forming around the metal. Loose pins must never be adjusted by nursing staff; any instability must be reported immediately, as a loose pin compromises traction efficacy and increases infection risks. Patient and family education regarding pin site care is also critical, especially if the patient is discharged with external fixators or pins. By adhering strictly to infection control principles, nurses safeguard patients against devastating bone infections.

headings.title: Patient Mobility and Complication Prevention
headings.content: Patient mobility is severely restricted during skeletal traction, presenting significant challenges that require proactive nursing interventions to prevent secondary complications. Prolonged bed rest places the patient at high risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, muscle atrophy, joint contractures, and pressure injuries. To combat DVT, nurses administer prescribed anticoagulants, apply compression stockings or sequential compression devices (SCDs) if permitted, and encourage ankle pumps and leg exercises within the limits of the traction apparatus. Although full ambulation is impossible, upper body exercises using an overhead trapeze bar allow the patient to lift their hips slightly for bed pan use and linen changes, which helps preserve upper body strength and promotes skin relief. Range-of-motion exercises for unaffected joints should be performed regularly to maintain joint flexibility and muscle tone. Bowel motility slows due to immobility and opioid analgesics, making a high-fiber diet, adequate hydration, and prescribed stool softeners essential to prevent constipation. Psychological support is equally important, as sensory deprivation and confinement can induce anxiety or depression. Nursing students must view the patient holistically, combining physical preventive measures with emotional encouragement to ensure the patient remains as active and complication-free as possible.

headings.title: Maintenance of Traction Weights and Alignment
headings.content: Maintaining traction weights and proper anatomical alignment is the core mechanical responsibility of the nurse managing skeletal traction. The prescribed weight amount must never be altered, added to, or removed by nursing staff without a direct physician order. All weights must hang freely suspended in the air, ensuring that the ropes do not catch on bed rails, footboards, bed linens, or medical equipment. Pulleys must be clean, lubricated, and moving freely to prevent friction that could reduce the effective pulling force on the bone. The patient's body alignment should be maintained in a straight line relative to the pull; pillows or rolled towels can be strategically placed to support the limb and prevent external rotation of the hip or foot drop. If the weights accidentally touch the floor or if a rope slips out of a pulley groove, the effective skeletal traction is lost, which can cause muscle spasms and disrupt bone healing. Nurses must conduct routine, systematic checks of the entire traction system at the start of every shift and after any patient movement. Educating family members not to touch, bump, or add items to the traction weights is also vital for maintaining therapeutic efficacy. Through diligent oversight of weights and alignment, nursing students ensure that the mechanical apparatus performs its therapeutic function uninterrupted.

headings.title: Discontinuation of Traction and Transition to Rehabilitation
headings.content: The discontinuation of skeletal traction marks a major milestone in the patient's orthopedic recovery and transitions them into the rehabilitation phase. Traction is typically discontinued when the orthopedic surgeon determines that sufficient callus formation and bone stability have occurred, or when transitioning to internal fixation, casting, or functional bracing. The removal of skeletal pins is a sterile procedure usually performed by the physician or trained nurse practitioner, often requiring local anesthesia or mild sedation to manage patient discomfort. Once the pins are removed, pin sites are cleansed and covered with sterile dressings until epithelialization is complete. The nurse plays a pivotal role in the transition phase by preparing the patient for mobilization, which often begins with dangle exercises, physical therapy consultations, and progressive weight-bearing as ordered. Muscle strengthening and joint range-of-motion exercises become the primary focus of care to reverse the effects of prolonged immobility. Pain management continues to be important as the patient adjusts to new appliances like casts or braces. Education regarding home care, warning signs of delayed infection, and activity restrictions ensures a safe discharge. Nursing students must understand this transition phase to support patients emotionally and physically as they regain independence and mobility.
